question: Given const MyContext = React.createContext(); MyContext.Provider, why might a consumer outside the Provider not receive context value?
options: Context only provides value to children inside Provider, outside consumers get undefined
Context broadcasts to all components globally
Consumers always receive value if context exists
Provider is optional for context
explanation: useContext() returns undefined if called outside a Provider; context value is only available to descendants of the specific Provider tree.

question: Why might useContext(MyContext) cause the entire component tree to re-render when the context value changes? const value = useMemo(() => ({ x }), [x]);
options: Context consumers subscribe to the entire value object; any change re-renders all consumers
useContext is memoized, no re-renders
Context changes are batched and optimized
Only the changed property re-renders
explanation: Context doesn't do fine-grained updates; changing any part of the context value re-renders all consumers, even if they don't use that part.

question: Given <Context.Provider value={{ x: 1, setX }}>, why might not memoizing the value cause children to re-render on every parent render?
options: New object on parent re-render, Context sees value changed, re-renders all consumers
Object identity is irrelevant for context
Context auto-memoizes values
Parent re-renders don't affect context consumers
explanation: {{ x: 1, setX }} creates a new object every render; Context compares with === and sees 'change', re-rendering all consumers even if x didn't change.

question: Why is creating multiple contexts better than one large context? const AuthContext = ...; const ThemeContext = ...;
options: Multiple contexts let consumers opt into only what they need, reducing unnecessary re-renders
One large context is always faster
Multiple contexts always cause more re-renders
Number of contexts doesn't matter
explanation: Multiple contexts allow components to subscribe to only relevant data; one large context causes all consumers to re-render when any part changes.

question: Given const value = useContext(MyContext); without a Provider, what does value become?
options: value is undefined (context has no default)
value is the default value passed to createContext
useContext throws an error
value is null
explanation: createContext(defaultValue) provides defaultValue if no Provider exists; useContext returns the default, not undefined (unless default is undefined).

question: Why might useContext not work inside a Provider of the same context? function Component() { const value = useContext(MyContext); return <MyContext.Provider value={value}> ... </MyContext.Provider>; }
options: Context nesting works; child Provider overrides parent value
useContext always reads the nearest Provider
Nested Providers cause errors
Context doesn't support nesting
explanation: Nested Providers work; useContext finds the nearest Provider in the component tree, so the child Provider overrides the parent for its descendants.

question: Given multiple useContext calls in one component: const x = useContext(Ctx1); const y = useContext(Ctx2);, why is this safe?
options: Multiple useContext calls are allowed, each subscribes to its context
Only one useContext per component is allowed
useContext calls must be in a specific order
Multiple contexts cause state conflicts
explanation: useContext can be called multiple times; each call subscribes to its own context independently, no conflicts or ordering issues.

question: Why might splitting context into separate files and consuming via hooks improve maintainability? export const useAuth = () => useContext(AuthContext);
options: Custom hook abstracts Provider location, allows easier refactoring
Context import/export is simple enough
Custom hooks add unnecessary complexity
This pattern provides no benefits
explanation: useAuth() hook encapsulates context access; if AuthContext moves or changes, only the hook needs updating, not every consumer component.

question: Given <Ctx.Provider value={value}><Child1 /><Child2 /></Ctx.Provider>, why might Child1 and Child2 have different context values after Parent re-render?
options: If value object is different, both children see the new value
Context provides different values to different children
Children always see the same context value
Parent re-renders don't affect context
explanation: Both children receive the same context value; if the value object is new (different reference), both re-render with the new value.

question: Why is splitting a context into [value, setValue] patterns better than combining them? export const [AuthContext, useAuth] = createContextPair();
options: Separate contexts prevent consumers needing setter from re-rendering on value changes
Single context is simpler
Separate contexts have no performance benefit
setValue should never be in context
explanation: If value and setter are in one context, components using only the setter still re-render when value changes; separate contexts avoid this waste.
